evidence: Catull. 61.23–25: quōs Hamādryades deae lūdicrum sibi rōscidō nūtriunt ūmōre
terms.comment: A thing to play with: in Catullus the myrtle sprigs that the wood-nymphs rear as a plaything for themselves (Lewis & Short: “a sport, toy, means of sport”). In prose lūdicrum is more often a show or public games (Livy). Morgan–Owens puts it first for “toy”, before lūdibrium. Plural lūdicra, lūdicrōrum.
Traupman’s word for a toy (p. 396); plural lūdibria, lūdibriōrum. In the authors lūdibrium is mockery, or a thing made sport of (lūdibria ventīs, playthings of the winds), so lūdicrum leads.

phrases.english: Which toy do you like best?
Pick up your toys; we’ll be having supper soon.

phrases.latin: quōs Hamādryades deae lūdicrum sibi rōscidō nūtriunt ūmōre
